subtopics.title: Finding lengths using ratios
subtopics.exposition: The hypotenuse is always the side opposite the right angle, and it never changes position. The opposite side is the side opposite the angle we are interested in, and the adjacent side is the remaining side. sin θ = opposite / hypotenuse. cos θ = adjacent / hypotenuse. tan θ = opposite / adjacent. Unknown lengths in right-angled triangles are found by using the trigonometric ratios. To find an unknown length, first identify the opposite and adjacent sides and the hypotenuse with reference to the given angle. Writing the sine ratio for the given 50° angle, with unknown side x and the hypotenuse 100, gives the equation sin 50° = x/100. When the unknown length x is divided by a known side, rearrange by multiplying both sides by that known side: sin 50° × 100 = x, so x = 100 sin 50°. After rearranging, use a calculator to find the answer: x = 100 sin 50° = 76.60444..., which rounds to 76.60. Writing the cosine ratio for the given 25° angle, with adjacent side 7 and unknown hypotenuse x, gives the equation cos 25° = 7/x. When the unknown length x is in the denominator, first multiply both sides by x: x cos 25° = 7. Then divide both sides by cos 25° to isolate x, giving x = 7 / cos 25°. Using a calculator, x = 7 / 0.90630... = 7.723645..., which rounds to 7.72. In a triangle with two unknown sides, x is found from the tangent ratio: tan 25° = x/7, so x = 7 × tan 25°. In the same triangle, y is found from the cosine ratio: cos 25° = 7/y, so y = 7 / cos 25°. When asked to round to two decimal places, the final length is written with the approximately-equal sign, for example x ≈ 76.60. The book writes the decimal mark as a comma, for example 76.60444...

subtopics.title: Finding angles using inverse ratios
subtopics.exposition: An inverse trigonometric function on the calculator works backwards: it uses the ratio of the sides to determine the angle which resulted in that ratio. If the lengths of two sides of a triangle are known, the angles can be calculated using trigonometric ratios. When the opposite side and the adjacent side for the angle θ are known, use the tangent ratio. Write the ratio of the known sides: with opposite 50 and adjacent 100, tan θ = 50/100. To solve for θ from tan θ = 50/100, use the inverse tangent function on the calculator. On the calculator, the inverse tangent is entered by pressing SHIFT and tan, then entering 50 ÷ 100 and pressing equals, which gives 26.56505... The final answer is written as an angle in degrees, θ ≈ 26.6°, using the degree symbol.

subtopics.title: Solving trigonometric equations
subtopics.exposition: Because 3 / 1.4 is greater than 1 and the maximum value of the cosine function is 1, cos α = 3 / 1.4 gives a calculator error and there is no solution. Both the sine and cosine functions have a maximum value of 1. The same techniques used for trigonometric equations in right-angled triangles can be used to solve trigonometric equations when the triangle is not shown. To solve cos θ = 0.2 for θ, use the inverse cosine function on the calculator. The inverse cosine is entered on the calculator by pressing SHIFT and cos, then entering 0.2, which gives 78.46304. The solution of cos θ = 0.2 is written as θ ≈ 78.46°. Before using the calculator, rearrange the equation so that the trigonometric ratio, for example sin θ, is on one side of the equation. Rearranging 3 sin θ = 2.4 gives sin θ = 2.4 / 3. To solve for θ from sin θ = 2.4/3, use the inverse sine function on the calculator. The inverse sine is entered on the calculator by pressing SHIFT and sin, then an opening bracket, then 2.4 ÷ 3, a closing bracket and equals, which gives 53.1301... The solution of 3 sin θ = 2.4 is written as θ ≈ 53.13°. There is no sec button on the calculator, so sec must be converted to cos before the angle can be found. The equation 3 sec α = 1.4 is converted to cosine form as 3 / cos α = 1.4. After converting, rearrange the equation so that cos α is on one side of the equation. From 3 / cos α = 1.4, multiplying both sides by cos α gives 3 = 1.4 cos α, and so 3 / 1.4 = cos α. When a calculator error occurs because the ratio is out of range, write 'no solution' and not 'math error'.

claims.claim: Unknown lengths in right-angled triangles are found by using the trigonometric ratios.
The hypotenuse is always the side opposite the right angle, and it never changes position.
The opposite side is the side opposite the angle we are interested in, and the adjacent side is the remaining side.
To find an unknown length, first identify the opposite and adjacent sides and the hypotenuse with reference to the given angle.
sin θ = opposite / hypotenuse.
cos θ = adjacent / hypotenuse.
tan θ = opposite / adjacent.
Writing the sine ratio for the given 50° angle, with unknown side x and the hypotenuse 100, gives the equation sin 50° = x/100.
When the unknown length x is divided by a known side, rearrange by multiplying both sides by that known side: sin 50° × 100 = x, so x = 100 sin 50°.
After rearranging, use a calculator to find the answer: x = 100 sin 50° = 76.60444..., which rounds to 76.60.
When asked to round to two decimal places, the final length is written with the approximately-equal sign, for example x ≈ 76.60.
The book writes the decimal mark as a comma, for example 76.60444...
Writing the cosine ratio for the given 25° angle, with adjacent side 7 and unknown hypotenuse x, gives the equation cos 25° = 7/x.
When the unknown length x is in the denominator, first multiply both sides by x: x cos 25° = 7.
Then divide both sides by cos 25° to isolate x, giving x = 7 / cos 25°.
Using a calculator, x = 7 / 0.90630... = 7.723645..., which rounds to 7.72.
In a triangle with two unknown sides, x is found from the tangent ratio: tan 25° = x/7, so x = 7 × tan 25°.
In the same triangle, y is found from the cosine ratio: cos 25° = 7/y, so y = 7 / cos 25°.
If the lengths of two sides of a triangle are known, the angles can be calculated using trigonometric ratios.
When the opposite side and the adjacent side for the angle θ are known, use the tangent ratio.
Write the ratio of the known sides: with opposite 50 and adjacent 100, tan θ = 50/100.
An inverse trigonometric function on the calculator works backwards: it uses the ratio of the sides to determine the angle which resulted in that ratio.
To solve for θ from tan θ = 50/100, use the inverse tangent function on the calculator.
On the calculator, the inverse tangent is entered by pressing SHIFT and tan, then entering 50 ÷ 100 and pressing equals, which gives 26.56505...
The final answer is written as an angle in degrees, θ ≈ 26.6°, using the degree symbol.
The same techniques used for trigonometric equations in right-angled triangles can be used to solve trigonometric equations when the triangle is not shown.
To solve cos θ = 0.2 for θ, use the inverse cosine function on the calculator.
The inverse cosine is entered on the calculator by pressing SHIFT and cos, then entering 0.2, which gives 78.46304.
The solution of cos θ = 0.2 is written as θ ≈ 78.46°.
Before using the calculator, rearrange the equation so that the trigonometric ratio, for example sin θ, is on one side of the equation.
Rearranging 3 sin θ = 2.4 gives sin θ = 2.4 / 3.
To solve for θ from sin θ = 2.4/3, use the inverse sine function on the calculator.
The inverse sine is entered on the calculator by pressing SHIFT and sin, then an opening bracket, then 2.4 ÷ 3, a closing bracket and equals, which gives 53.1301...
The solution of 3 sin θ = 2.4 is written as θ ≈ 53.13°.
There is no sec button on the calculator, so sec must be converted to cos before the angle can be found.
The equation 3 sec α = 1.4 is converted to cosine form as 3 / cos α = 1.4.
After converting, rearrange the equation so that cos α is on one side of the equation.
From 3 / cos α = 1.4, multiplying both sides by cos α gives 3 = 1.4 cos α, and so 3 / 1.4 = cos α.
Because 3 / 1.4 is greater than 1 and the maximum value of the cosine function is 1, cos α = 3 / 1.4 gives a calculator error and there is no solution.
When a calculator error occurs because the ratio is out of range, write 'no solution' and not 'math error'.
When solving a trigonometric equation, an error from the calculator when calculating sin or cos means there is no solution to the equation.
Both the sine and cosine functions have a maximum value of 1.
